Salesforce https://www.salesforce.com/blog/ Learn how to get ahead of trends and supercharge professional relationships Fri, 20 Nov 2026 23:10:52 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.1.5 https://www.salesforce.com/blog/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2020/10/cropped-salesforce-icon2-1.png?w=32 Salesforce https://www.salesforce.com/blog/ 32 32 218238330 25 Practical Jobs Organizations are Giving Agentforce Coworker to Complete Right Now https://www.salesforce.com/blog/agentforce-coworker-practical-jobs/ https://www.salesforce.com/blog/agentforce-coworker-practical-jobs/#respond Fri, 20 Nov 2026 23:10:49 +0000 https://www.salesforce.com/?p=161409 You know those tasks that somehow eat up half your day? Digging through 14 tabs before a customer call. Writing the same weekly update for the 47th time. Hunting down one record that should take 30 seconds to find. The list goes on.

Turns out, teams are handing them off to Agentforce Coworker and are getting hours back in their day in return. Agentforce Coworker is the autonomous AI teammate that puts Salesforce to work for you. It knows your business context, orchestrates Agentforce agents to take action on your behalf, and follows the permissions and governance rules your company already trusts. 

We rounded up 25 jobs organizations are delegating and asking Coworker to finish right now. We give you full permission to steal them shamelessly for your next task.

For sales teams

1. Kick-offs ready in a day, not a week: Coworker pulls the pre-sale notes, opportunity history, contract terms, and email threads into one kick-off brief for you to review. Kick-offs that took 4 to 5 business days to prepare now happen within 24 hours of closing.

Try this prompt: “Pull CRM notes, opportunity details, and any contract records for [Account], and draft a kick-off brief.”

2. The follow-up email that writes itself: Drop in your raw call notes. Coworker drafts the follow-up from the deal history on the opportunity and contact, then logs the activity and updates the stage once you approve. 

Try this prompt: “Draft a follow-up email to [Contact] at [Account] summarizing our discussion on [topic] and confirming next steps. Here are my raw notes: [paste notes]. Update the opportunity stage and log the activity.”

3. The one-page briefing: One page now replaces 12 tabs. Before a client call, Coworker pulls recent calls and emails, open cases, and opportunity notes, plus the email and calendar around the account, and adds talking points. It only shows what you have access to. Prep that took 10 to 15 minutes is now a single prompt.

Try this prompt: “Help me prepare for my meeting tomorrow with [Account], including recent interactions, open opportunities, unresolved questions, customer concerns, and recommended talking points.”

4. Get ready for a new offer: Launching a bundle? Coworker finds the accounts that qualify and the open quotes that need updating, has agents revise them, and drafts the announcements. You approve before anything goes out.

Try this prompt: “For my open quotes and accounts, check that [bundle] is added to relevant opportunities, flag any quotes missing it, and identify accounts that are a good fit based on [criteria].”

5. Deal Desk sign-off without the chase: Hand Coworker the approval and it sends the deal terms from the opportunity and quote to your Deal Desk agent, then brings back the decision. No emails, no re-explaining the deal.

Try this prompt: “Create a Deal Desk case for the three-year term on [Account] and notify the right team.”

6. Log the call from your phone: Walking out of a meeting, tell Coworker the terms, the deadline, and who your champion is. It updates the opportunity and contact role, moves the stage, and confirms before saving. Your CRM is current before the next meeting.

Try this prompt: “Log it: three-year term, legal by the 20th, [Contact] is our champion. Move it to Negotiation.”

For account and customer success teams

7. Run the incident playbook on your book: The Skill your company built runs for every rep when a product issue hits customers. Coworker finds your affected accounts, ranks them by risk using renewal, escalation, and expansion data, and drafts the emails and call briefs for your approval. In the launch demo, eight accounts were ranked, with six emails and two call briefs ready to approve.

Try this prompt: “Pull accounts in my book flagged for [churn risk / renewal risk / specific criteria] and draft outreach for each.”

8. Recover an at-risk renewal, end to end: Nobody likes finding out an account is unhappy when it is already halfway out the door. Coworker pulls the contract, service history, and unresolved cases, brings in the right agents for terms and follow-up, and returns the work for your approval.

Try this prompt: “[Account]’s renewal is at risk. Pull the service history, find the unresolved cases, and prepare the customer follow-up.”

9. The account recap you didn’t have to read 40 emails for: Coworker reads the account’s CRM activity, cases, email, and Slack threads, writes the recap, drafts next steps, and updates your custom fields once you approve using field API names. Reviews that took 30 to 45 minutes now take just a few minutes.

Try this prompt: “Summarize the last 90 days of activity with [Account], including calls, emails, meetings, and open tasks. Draft next steps and update the custom summary fields.”

10. The “never leave this screen” account review: Compare two promotions, check the customer’s sentiment score, and fix a wrong phone number in one pass, all on the same account. No tab-hopping, and the next outreach rests on accurate details.

Try this prompt: “Compare [Promotion A] and [Promotion B] for [Account], show the customer’s sentiment score, and update the contact’s phone number to [number].”

11. Prep the call and book it: Coworker turns the renewal, open escalation, and pending expansion into talking points you can trust, then books the call through your connected calendar.

Try this prompt: “Prep me for my call with [Account], then book it.”

12. Meeting notes into follow-up tasks: Coworker pulls the action items out of your logged meeting notes, with owners and due dates where it can, and creates the follow-up tasks once you approve. Nothing falls through the cracks.

Try this prompt: “Summarize my customer meetings from last week, extract the action items with owners and due dates, and create follow-up tasks for the open ones.”

For sales leaders and managers

13. Get every slipping deal moving: Coworker works through your pipeline in the background, spots deals at risk from stage, close date, and last activity, asks the Deal Desk agent for terms on stalled ones, and flags where an executive sponsor could help. You see where to step in.

Try this prompt: “Find at-risk deals and for each one, draft an outreach email, suggest a next step, and create a follow-up task.”

14. Skip the custom report, just ask: Ask for the info you need, in the format you need it. Coworker reads the same data a report would, within your own permissions. No new reports, no special automation, and nothing added to the dev backlog.

Try this prompt: “Show me [metric] by [dimension] for [team] as a table, sorted by [field].”

15. Turn your best playbook into a Skill: A top rep’s renewal playbook can become how the whole team runs renewals. Save a workflow as a Skill, share it, and anyone can run it in one line, with the same steps and agents every time, within their own permissions.

Try this prompt: “Make this a skill.”

16. A risk briefing waiting for Monday’s meeting: Coming soon, scheduled tasks let Coworker run recurring work on its own. Set up a weekly risk briefing once and it is ready before the meeting every week, drawn from live opportunity, case, and activity data.

Try this prompt: “Save this as a skill I can run each Monday morning.”

For marketers

17. The Monday campaign check: One team spent 90 minutes every Monday digging through sync errors and writing the update. Coworker now flags the lead and campaign member records with missing or bad fields and drafts the summary. The team reviews it in about 25 minutes.

Try this prompt: “Pull last week’s campaign member and lead changes, flag records missing [specific fields], and draft a summary with next actions.”

18. Fix the bad records, not just find them: After Coworker flags records with missing or bad fields, ask it to propose the fixes. It updates the flagged records only after you approve, so you review instead of editing one by one.

Try this prompt: “For the records you flagged with missing or bad fields, propose the corrections and update them once I approve.”

For operations teams

19. Sprint reviews in 15 minutes: Coworker watches for updates across your team’s tools (connected through Data 360), flags bottlenecks, and drafts the report. Prep that took 90 minutes now takes 15, saving 75 minutes per sprint.

Try this prompt: “Summarize this sprint’s updates from CRM and Slack, flag bottlenecks, and draft the review report.”

20. Reschedule installs and hold shipments: When an incident touches orders, Coworker finds every affected order, has the field service agent reschedule installs, and queues shipment holds. Nothing moves without your sign-off.

Try this prompt: “Find all orders for [product], update the install date field to [new date], and create approval requests for shipment holds.”

21. Triage open cases and update the records: Coworker reads the open cases tied to an incident, flags the ones closest to breaching SLA, drafts a reply for each, and updates the records. You review and send, so the most urgent customers hear back first.

Try this prompt: “Show me my open cases tied to the incident, flag the ones closest to breaching SLA, and draft a reply for each.”

For admins and security teams

22. Debugging and research: Coworker already understands your org’s classes, flows, and configuration, so it explains errors against your own setup. Debugging and research that took 1 to 2 hours is now often 20 to 30 minutes.

Try this prompt: “Explain this error: [paste]. Search our knowledge base and Slack for known causes, and tell me which flows or classes to investigate.”

23. Root-cause hunting: Coworker surfaces the classes and flows around a production issue, so you start from a short list instead of a blank search. One developer estimates it saves 3 to 4 hours a week.

Try this prompt: “Show me the classes and flows involved in [process] that could be causing [production issue].”

24. Finding the record in record speed: Coworker searches your org’s objects and fields directly, with your permissions, so you skip the report-building step. Finding a record that took up to 45 minutes now takes about 5.

Try this prompt: “Find the [object] record where [known details], and show its owner and last modified date.”

25. Audit access after an incident: After an incident, ask Coworker to audit access on the affected accounts. It scans permissions across Salesforce and Data 360, flags over-provisioned users and unrevoked temporary grants, and traces each to its source. A weeks-long audit becomes an on-demand answer, and nothing changes without a human.

Try this prompt: “Audit access on the incident accounts.” Then: “Why does each one have access?”

What makes Coworker unique?

Most general-purpose AI tools help you find answers, generate content, or complete individual tasks. Coworker goes a step further. It’s designed to understand your business and help get work done, right where your teams already work.

Here is how that plays out.

It understands your business. Instead of starting from scratch, Coworker works with the data and context already in Salesforce, including your accounts, cases, contracts, and business rules. Built on Data 360 and Agentforce, it can also access data from more than 330 additional sources through zero copy.

It goes beyond answering questions. Coworker can plan and carry out tasks using flows, APIs, and specialized agents. It can work in the background or on a schedule, then bring the results back for your review.

It’s easy to get started. There’s no need to build custom connectors or data pipelines to get started with its built-in capabilities. Admins can enable Coworker in Salesforce Setup and assign access to the right people.

It works within your existing security controls. Coworker respects each user’s Salesforce permissions, requests approval before saving or sending information, and logs its actions so teams have visibility into what’s happening.

It works where you do. Whether you’re in Salesforce, Microsoft Teams, or supported mobile, desktop, and MCP applications, Coworker lets you work across tools without constantly starting over.


Your turn

You’ve seen 25 ways teams are putting Agentforce Coworker to work, now it’s your turn. Ready to experience your new favorite coworker? You can turn it on in two minutes.

  1. Go to Salesforce Setup
  2. Search for “Agentforce Coworker”
  3. Toggle it on

That’s it! Then pick the one task that makes you groan every time it lands on your calendar, and hand it over. Your future self (and your calendar) will thank you.

Now comes a choice that shapes your results as much as the technology: who will help you get the most value from it? We know that real value comes when it works across the business, with the right context, no matter what new technology arrives or what customers have already invested in. One of the key steps to success? Finding the right partner.

The Salesforce Partner Ecosystem includes global systems integrators (GSIs) with tens of thousands of consultants, and boutique firms with a few dozen specialists. No single partner is “best” and we’re not ones to pick favorites, unless it’s our favorite character (in which case it’s Codey.) The right one for you depends on your size, your industry, and what you need after launch. 

This post walks you through those three questions. Start at the top, answer honestly, and you’ll end up with a short list worth talking to. Grab your pencil, break out the notes app, and let’s begin.

Question 1: How big and complex is your organization?

Size comes first because it sets the kind of delivery team you need.

Large enterprise? Start with the large SIs. That usually means several business units, multiple Salesforce apps, dozens of integrations, and users in many regions. You need a partner that can:

  • Staff a large program and run a global delivery model
  • Coordinate teams across finance, IT, sales, service, and marketing
  • Has experience managing change and adoption across the whole organization

Large SIs also have deep ties across the ecosystem, which helps when your project involves ERP, data platforms, or older systems.

Things to consider: How quickly do you need to move,  who will be on your team day to day, not just who joins the pitch, and who is the project manager at your organization. 

Mid-sized company? Look at regional and mid-sized SIs. They often strike the best balance. They have the depth for a multi-cloud rollout, and they work with companies like yours every day, so your project gets real focus.

Small or growing business? A boutique or specialist firm is usually a great fit. You’ll often get senior people on your project, direct access to decision makers, and pricing that fits your scale.

Question 2: What industry are you in, and how regulated is it?

For many customers, this question matters most, and it can outweigh the first.

If you work in financial services, healthcare, life sciences, the public sector, or another regulated industry, put industry experience first. Regulations shape your data model, access controls, consent management, audit trails, and how you can use customer data, including with AI. A partner who has done this before will identify hurdles early. A partner who hasn’t may figure it out on your time and at your cost.

Here’s what to look for:

  • Financial services: Experience with data residency, privacy and consent rules, record retention, and security reviews. Ask how they’ve handled know-your-customer (KYC) workflows, advisor and customer relationship models, and integration with core banking or policy systems.
  • Healthcare and life sciences: Familiarity with patient privacy requirements, validated systems, and the compliance processes for working with providers and patients.
  • Public sector: Knowledge of procurement rules, security authorizations, and accessibility standards.

Industry depth matters outside regulated sectors too. In manufacturing, for example, look for experience with dealer and partner networks, complex orders and quotes, connected-product data, and ERP integration. A partner who knows manufacturing will understand how Salesforce fits with the systems that run your plants and supply chain.

In any industry, a partner with strong sector experience can outperform a larger generalist. You don’t have to choose between big and specialized. Ask for both.

Question 3: Defining your goals after go-live

It’s easy to focus on the build and forget what comes next. Before you sign, decide how you want to be supported after launch and really define your outcomes with your partner. 

  • Strong in-house Salesforce team? Look for a partner who builds, shares what they know, and continues to support your transformation. 
  • Limited in-house capacity? Look for managed services, ongoing improvements, and a clear way to add new capabilities as your business needs grow over time. 

Either way, ask how knowledge transfer will work and what documentation you’ll get.

Test your short list

Once you have a handful of firms, ask each one the same questions:

  1. Who will do the work? Meet the proposed team and learn about their experience, not just the firm’s.
  2. Can we talk to customers like us? References in your industry, at your size, and on your clouds tell you more than a polished case study.
  3. How do you measure success? Look for partners who talk about business results, like faster cycle times, higher adoption, and lower costs to serve, as well as on-time delivery.
  4. What happens when plans change? Every project has surprises. A good partner can tell you how they handled a shift in scope or a delay.
  5. How do you approach data and AI readiness? Strong AI results depend on clean, connected data. A partner who brings this up early is thinking about your long-term success.

You’re choosing a partner, not just a vendor

The best partnerships feel like an extension of your team. You share goals, talk openly about tradeoffs, and care about what happens after launch.

Use the tree to find the right size, expertise, and support model. Then trust your read of the people. You’ll work with them for months or years, and that relationship matters as much as any credential.

Fix Your Knowledge Articles First https://www.salesforce.com/blog/how-to-write-knowledge-articles/ https://www.salesforce.com/blog/how-to-write-knowledge-articles/#respond Fri, 20 Nov 2026 18:45:06 +0000 https://www.salesforce.com/?p=161359 As service organizations embrace autonomous AI, expectations have skyrocketed. Leaders are counting on AI agents to resolve inquiries, guide customers through complex troubleshooting, and take routine work off service reps’ plates. And the momentum is real: 40% of case resolution interactions involving AI are now completed entirely autonomously.

There’s just one catch: an AI agent is only as reliable as the knowledge that powers it.

When your AI agent accesses your knowledge base, it doesn’t read the library from top to bottom before answering a customer. It retrieves the sections that best match the question and generates an answer from them.

If critical conditions are buried in step eight of an old call-center script, or if four unrelated procedures are crammed into one long article, the agent will miss the point. To unlock the full power of agentic AI, service teams must stop writing for human eyes alone and start writing knowledge that AI can ground on.

How AI agents process knowledge

Traditional knowledge bases were built for service reps who could skim past fluff, interpret corporate jargon, and connect dots across pages. When an AI agent queries your documentation, it operates under three fundamental dynamics:

  1. Retrieve a slice: In a typical RAG setup, the unit of retrieval is a chunk — often returning multiple relevant passages rather than a single static page. Clear headings and self-contained sections help preserve the meaning of each chunk when it is pulled into the model’s context.
  2. Context-driven generation: Depending on the query and policy, an AI agent must either return exact parameters or adapt multi-step instructions to fit the customer’s specific situation. In either case, critical details buried deep in dense paragraphs are easily missed during retrieval.
  3. Strict adherence to source text: An AI agent can adapt how it phrases an answer, but it can only work with what your article says. If a fee, eligibility requirement or security exception isn’t written down, the agent has nothing reliable to ground on.

In the AI era, articles serve two vital jobs: they ground direct answers to factual queries, and they act as an immediate safety net — allowing the AI agent to surface the right step-by-step article directly to the customer (or to a human rep during a handoff) whenever it can’t complete an action autonomously.

The golden rule: write once, completely, and audience-neutral

The foundational rule for AI agent-ready content is straightforward: the article is the source; the agent is the behavior.

That means a knowledge article should be an objective, persona-free reference. It should never contain scripted greetings, empathy statements, confirmation prompts, or live-agent escalation scripts. Persona, tone, and conversational pacing belong in the agent’s instructions, rather than in the article body.

If a draft reads like a polished, chatty customer FAQ, it’s likely missing the technical precision the agent needs. A RAG-ready (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) article should be thorough, leaving no assumption unstated, with clear headings to keep it quick to scan.

Actionable suggestions to make your knowledge AI-ready

To get the best performance from your AI agents, your content needs to be engineered for accurate retrieval and clean interpretation — not just human skimming. Apply these core practices across your knowledge base, then use the rubric below to score and prioritize your existing articles.

1. Scope and structure for clean retrieval

  • Focus on one customer intent per article: Avoid multi-topic blobs. Group questions by distinct customer intent or workflow rather than arbitrary page counts so chunks from different procedures don’t blur into a single confusing answer.
  • Lead with the answer and optimize metadata: Place the direct resolution at the very top, and treat your Title and Summary fields as primary retrieval signals.
  • Use shallow, sequential headings (<h2>–<h4>): Use real heading tags rather than bold text, and keep hierarchy sequential without skipping levels (e.g., don’t jump from <h2> to <h4>). Make each section self-contained—avoid backward references like “as mentioned above,” and briefly restate essential prerequisites so any retrieved chunk stands cleanly on its own.
  • Govern search with a Data Category taxonomy: Use Salesforce Knowledge Data Categories (such as product, region, or segment) to establish a structured taxonomy that filters search queries before generation. As Gartner highlights in its Knowledge Management evaluations, a disciplined taxonomy prevents AI agents from pulling conflicting or out-of-scope policies across similar topics.
  • Author or sync in clean Markdown when possible: AI agents parse Markdown (.md) natively and reliably, giving retrieval engines crisp structural boundaries without heavy HTML styling overhead.

2. Write with explicit precision (zero guesswork)

  • Include complete conditions without padding: Detail all edge cases, eligibility rules, and exceptions directly in the text without conversational fluff. Strip out human agent scripts and routing logic (like “Apologize and transfer to Tier 2”) so internal behavior doesn’t leak into customer-facing responses.
  • Place prerequisites and warnings before the action: Put data-loss warnings or required permissions before the step that triggers them, never at the bottom of the page.
  • Make conditional logic and numbers unambiguous: Write branching paths explicitly (“If X, do Y; otherwise, do Z”), and separate materially different workflows under clear labels (e.g., “For SSO users” vs. “For password users”). Spell out exact units, currencies, time zones, and trigger events—write “The code expires 10 minutes after it is issued” rather than “expires shortly.”
  • Use explicit UI labels instead of visual cues: Name the exact control and action (“Select Save” rather than “Click the green button on the right”), and keep error codes, commands, and sample values in selectable text or code formatting rather than locked inside screenshots.
  • Embed caller language and descriptive links: Define acronyms inline (e.g., “SSO / single sign-on”), include a “Common questions this article answers” block using real case-subject phrasing, and use descriptive link text (“Password eligibility requirements” instead of “Click here”) while keeping core task requirements inline.

3. Format text and media for machine parsing

  • Use numbered lists for sequences: Use actual editor list formatting with one main action per step, stating where the action happens and the expected confirmation result.
  • Keep tables simple and labeled: Favor numbered lists for procedures, and when you do use tables, stick to proper header cells, clear row/column labels, and a brief prose takeaway — avoiding merged or nested cells.
  • Make visual and audio content readable in text: Keep essential instructions in the article body so screenshots only supplement the text. Add descriptive alt text to informative images (and alt=”” to decorative ones), summarize chart or diagram takeaways in nearby prose, and provide captions and transcripts with key visual actions for video or audio.

Audit your library with the 20-point readiness rubric

Once you know what good looks like, score a sample of your highest-volume articles (0 = Missing, 1 = Partial, 2 = Complete) to pinpoint where to focus first:

How to evaluate your score and plan next steps:

  • 16–20 (Considered RAG-Ready): A strong candidate for indexing, subject to critical checks and retrieval/response evaluation.
  • 10–15 (Potential for Improvement): Needs targeted edits — try splitting off extra topics, tightening conditional phrasing, or pulling buried prerequisites into their own headings.
  • 0–9 (Candidate for Redesign): Focus on legacy scripts or monolithic guides. It is often best to rebuild these using standalone templates before exposing them to the agent.

These architectural practices apply wherever your content lives. With Enterprise Knowledge, AI agents can ground answers across external repositories like Google Drive, SharePoint, and Confluence — meaning structured, chunk-ready content pays off across all your content sources.

Before and after: rebuilding a legacy support guide for AI

Here’s how those principles transform a typical monolithic support guide into clean, agent-ready knowledge:

By separating topics and surfacing rules under clear headers, the agent can retrieve the exact slice of information it needs — which reduces the risk of incorrect or incomplete answers and ensures it must not invent unsupported details. Paired with ongoing retrieval testing and up-to-date content, clean structure keeps procedures distinct and reliable.

Treat knowledge as a living asset — and invest in it

Knowledge management isn’t a one-time migration — it’s an ongoing operational discipline. Even the cleanest article architecture will produce outdated answers if the underlying policies go stale, and keeping hundreds of articles current by hand quickly becomes a bottleneck.

That is where Service Cloud turns knowledge maintenance into a closed-loop system:

  • Spot gaps and decay proactively with Knowledge Health: Instead of guessing which articles are dragging down agent performance, use Knowledge Health to continuously monitor article quality, identify outdated or underperforming content, and pinpoint duplicates or structural blind spots before they impact customers.
  • Turn customer signals into new drafts with Self-Learning Knowledge: Self-Learning Knowledge analyzes incoming cases, conversations, and interactions alongside your existing knowledge base to automatically detect content gaps and generate draft articles grounded in real resolutions.
  • Close the loop on every escalation: In Service Cloud, treat customer escalations, bot handoffs, and unanswered questions as your content team’s direct to-do list. When an agent stumbles, don’t just tweak prompts — update, republish, and re-index the underlying article.

By pairing AI agents with clean, structured, and well-maintained knowledge, your service organization can confidently turn self-service into your highest-performing channel.

Each blog shares real-world examples of solving data problems and best practices learned along the way. The opinions shared are our own — and written without AI.

Choosing the right agent, for the right use case


Recently, we were working with one of our large enterprise customers in a highly regulated industry, who had set out to rethink how their people get answers from data. For years, the routine at the company had been the same: log in to Tableau, find the right project, open a dashboard, and use dynamic filters and parameters to answer a question. While dashboards still have their place, user expectations are shifting, and agents are fundamentally changing how people expect to engage with data.

Tableau Cloud and Server are often the source of truth for enterprise data, including the last-mile logic business users add in Tableau (calculations, groups, descriptions, etc.) that rarely makes it into the warehouse. Tableau MCP lets an agent query that data and logic, and external tools allow that same agent to act on what it finds. That raises the stakes on trust and governance, especially in a regulated industry where taking action on a wrong answer can become a compliance issue. It’s a concern many organizations share: in McKinsey’s 2026 AI trust survey, 74% named inaccuracy as a highly relevant AI risk, and nearly two-thirds said security and risk concerns are the top barrier to scaling agentic AI.

Before any development work began with this customer, we first collaborated with their engineering team to decide what type of agent to deploy, and for which use case. Tableau offers several ready-to-use agents, such as Tableau Agent for preparing data and exploring dashboards and Tableau Agent in Pulse for asking questions of defined metrics. These agents are tightly scoped to improve accuracy out of the box, and for broad Q&A inside Tableau, they’re a great place to start.

But this specific customer needed more, due to specific requirements:

  • Specialized workflows: They needed agents that answer a very specific subset of questions, where accuracy was paramount. 
  • Agentic workflows: Users needed to act on what they found in Tableau without leaving the agent. Our first agent dealt with supply chain delays: spotting a delayed part, then locating alternate suppliers. That only works if Tableau and the ERP share the same definitions and identifiers.
  • Embedding outside Tableau: Their users lived in a purpose-built application, so the agents had to operate within that environment.
  • Full control and oversight: Their developers wanted more fine-grained control. They wanted to control what data each agent could see, which tools and prompts it used, and which questions it should answer or refuse. 
  • Proof before production: In the highly regulated industry they operate in, probably right wasn’t good enough. Every agent had to be tested and proven before it ever reached the end users.

This led us to build custom agents with Tableau MCP. This gave the customer control that a ready-to-use agent couldn’t, but that control also demands more rigorous testing, tighter governance and ongoing monitoring. The six practices below are what helped take the customer’s agents from prototype to production.

Step 1: Prepare the data model

This step applies to any agent, ready-to-use or custom, and everything else builds on top of it. Any agent can only be as accurate as the data model it reads. Optimizing the data model, cleaning up metadata, and adding business logic improves agent accuracy, reduces token spend, and speeds up response time.

Before configuring an agent, we recommend these steps:

1. First, decide where the logic should live: For each piece of business logic, we recommend putting it as close to the data as possible.

    • If the logic can be written as a calculation, write a calculated field so it gives the same answer each time and isn’t left to agent interpretation. For example, Open Pipeline should be  IF NOT [Stage] IN (‘Closed Won’, ‘Closed Lost’) THEN [Opportunity Amount] END.
    • If it’s logic that every agent should know, put it within Tableau Knowledge business preferences, or within field descriptions. For example, “active pipeline,” and “opportunities in-flight” should both map to Open Pipeline.
    • If it’s logic that only applies to a single agent, put it in that agent’s system instructions. For example, an agent exclusive to sales leadership might default to this quarter’s Open Pipeline by region, while a rep-facing agent on the same data defaults to the rep’s own deals.

    2. Remove any field duplicates: Oftentimes, analyst experimentation when modeling data leads to duplicative fields. Make sure you keep only one version of each measure or dimension, and hide or delete the rest.

    3. Describe the fields: Descriptions are what an agent reads when it decides which field to use. We recommend adding short descriptions with units, grain and caveats, such as whether Net Revenue includes returns. 

    4. Name fields based upon the business logic: Use field names people refer to (e.g., “Net Revenue”), not database names (e.g., “rev_net_adj”) or slang.

    5. Hide irrelevant fields: Extraneous fields including IDs, join keys, and duplicative calculations only give the agent more ways to go wrong.

    6. Certify the data source: Mark the data sources the agent is allowed to rely on.

      New: Automate your metadata with the TDS Edit API. Available in Tableau Cloud (October 2026) and Tableau Server 2026.3, the new TDS Edit methods in the Tableau REST API let you add and update field and table descriptions in code.

      Step 2: Define the agent’s role

      An open-ended agent pointed at a broad schema necessitates both understanding the question and finding the data source that holds the answer. Removing the second step reduces the risk of a wrong answer and can speed up agent response time.

      Before any agent went into production, we challenged the customer to answer four questions:

      1. What problem is it solving? For example: Operations managers currently spend hours each week pulling site performance from several dashboards.
      2. What domain is it serving? For example: Site operations, using the certified operations performance Published Data Source.
      3. What can and can’t it answer? For example: It should only answer questions related to site targets, output and downtime. It should refuse questions related to HR, finance or individual employees.
      4. How should it answer? For example: This is for operational purposes. Report only the numbers and provide no interpretation. 

      The answers then decide which data and tools the agent gets, and form the core of its system prompt.

      New in 2026.3: Tableau MCP supports embedded data sources. Your agent can now also query a data source embedded within a workbook. That means the agent can reuse the calculations, parameters and groups your analysts have already built and validated.

      Step 3: Follow the principle of least privilege


      It is tempting to expand an agent’s capabilities by leaving extra tools enabled and connecting additional data sources, but each added capability brings new failure modes. The principle of least privilege is a long-standing security practice: give a system access to only what it needs to do its job, and nothing more. This principle is critical when using agents, as an agent decides at runtime which tools to call, and every tool you leave enabled is one it can use, or be talked into using, in ways you didn’t plan for.

      So once we had defined the agent’s role, we then removed every tool it didn’t need, starting with list-datasources. The list-datasources tool lets an agent browse every data source on the site. Instead, we gave it the specific ID of the data source it should use in its system prompt. This matters for three reasons:

      • Accuracy: the agent doesn’t risk querying a similar, yet incorrect, source to answer a question.
      • Speed and cost: every tool the agent doesn’t call saves a step and the token consumption that comes along with it.
      • Governance: the agent can only reach the data you’ve approved for its role.

      We then enforced those limits within Tableau MCP itself, so a user can’t get around them by pasting a different data source ID into the chat. Tableau MCP’s tool scoping settings control which tools and data sources an agent can reach. Where you set them depends on how you run Tableau MCP:

      • Hosted Tableau MCP (Tableau Cloud): a site admin applies them through site settings, as described here.

      Note: If your agent uses an embedded data source, scope it by project or tag instead, since INCLUDE_DATASOURCE_IDS blocks embedded data sources entirely.

      Step 4 (optional): Load metadata into the system prompt upfront

      We noticed that the agent knew which data source to use, but still called the get-datasource-metadata tool at the start of each session. This lookup added noticeable latency.

      To combat this, we borrowed a technique from our internal Tableau MCP demos inside Slack, which involves using a skill containing the data source LUID and a snapshot of the field-level metadata. This greatly reduced the time to respond to our initial queries and stopped our agent from veering off-course with an incorrect dataset. The problem is that while the technique works great in a one-off demo, it is not so great in production, as field-level metadata can change at any time. 

      To improve the response time and remove the risk of a stale snapshot, we pulled the metadata from Tableau when the agent started, inserted it into the system prompt dynamically, and removed the get-datasource-metadata tool altogether. This means the agent now starts every question already knowing the current fields, which reduced our response time by almost 50%.

      This approach worked for our use case, but it has trade-offs. The main one is how tightly scoped your agent is. If an agent has access to more than one or two data sources, it likely makes more sense to restore the get-datasource-metadata tool, so that it can resolve field-level information at runtime. A given question usually needs only one data source, and loading the full schemas of four or five sources upfront adds token consumption and latency to every request.

      The other, smaller trade-off is freshness. Because the metadata is loaded into the prompt when the agent starts, a mid-session change to the data source leaves the agent working from a stale copy, and you’ve removed its ability to fetch updates. For us, that risk was negligible: the data source was locked, and any modification had to go through a well governed process, so the metadata couldn’t change unexpectedly. Yet, if your metadata changes frequently, consider keeping the get-datasource-metadata tool available, with strict instructions to use it only when something looks wrong.

      Step 5: Pre-build queries for known questions 

      Once the customer’s agents were in use, we noticed many of the same questions coming up repeatedly. Each time, this required the agent to rebuild the query, choosing the appropriate fields, filters and calculations, which consumed unnecessary tokens and opened up another chance for error.

      For these known questions, we recommend not relying on the agent to build the query at all. A developer can write and test the query once and add it to the agent as a custom tool. So when an employee asks a common question like “How many days off do I have left?”, the agent calls that tool with the signed-in employee’s ID, and the model only has to explain the result. That improves accuracy and cuts down extraneous token usage.

      How far to take this is a judgment call that depends on the stakes. We ultimately recommend against chasing 100% accuracy from an agent. If a question needs that level of certainty, like an FP&A figure that feeds a financial report, build a dashboard. If you want breadth and agility, like an AE building a sales plan, build an agent, pre-build queries where possible, and accept some level of ambiguity.

      Step 6: Build an agent evaluation and monitoring framework

      Unlike a deterministic dashboard, an agent doesn’t always give the same answer the same way each time. A small change, such as rewording the system prompt, switching models, or adding a tool, can fix one answer and quietly break another. In this customer’s case, due to regulatory scrutiny, the team wanted to ensure they could catch any errors before an agent ever reached production. This led to a governance framework that can be broken down into several steps:

      1. Start with a question bank: We developed a list of questions users were asking, each paired with the correct answer. In this case, we started with the questions the team defined in step 2 above, and the questions it should refuse.
      2. Test configurations: Using an evaluation tool, such as LangSmith, we ran the question bank against different versions of the agent, including different prompts, models and settings. Each run measured the accuracy, latency and token usage. For this specific customer, accuracy was the priority, but other teams may decide to trade long instructions covering every edge case, for an agent that is faster and cheaper to run.
      3. Evaluate response quality: With accuracy testing in place, we began grading answers for less deterministic questions like, “How is my territory looking this quarter?” or, “Is there anything I should worry about with tomorrow’s outgoing shipments?” For this, we used the common approach of an “LLM as a judge” where we used a second model to evaluate the quality of the response, when given examples of the chosen style and format. Small classification models like Jev are a fast, low-cost option for this type of evaluation.
      4. Treat every change like a software release: We versioned the prompts and settings, and ran the full bank of questions before any change went live. In many ways this mirrors the way developers run tests before shipping code.
      5. Monitor in production: We then ensured we could track response time, token usage, tool failures and how often people use the agent. If the agent becomes mission-critical, we’d advise considering high availability and disaster recovery, as you would for any other critical enterprise application.
      6. Establish an ongoing maintenance process: Users will inevitably ask questions the bank doesn’t cover. We made sure there was a regular review of what users were asking using the agent’s logs or traces, and then added new questions to the bank along with their correct answers. When a wrong answer comes from an unclear field, fix the field’s description in the data source and run the bank again.

      Above is a screenshot of the harness we built to test and improve agents tasked with using Tableau MCP. It turned out to be far more complicated than we originally anticipated. For that reason, we recommend using an established agent observability platform.

      What we learned

      Going through this process reinforced several key principles:

      • It starts with the data model. Tableau customers already have valuable logic in their published data sources and workbooks. Putting that logic in the right place, and keeping the data model clean, is paramount to letting agents work reliably.
      • Setup matters more than the model. An agent’s accuracy depends far more on how it’s set up, configured and maintained.
      • Narrow scope improves accuracy. Limiting the data an agent can access, the tools it uses, and the questions it answers makes it more accurate.
      • Production agents need enterprise discipline. Like any other enterprise application, an agent needs versioning, testing and ongoing monitoring.

      None of these principles is difficult on its own. The harder part is the ongoing maintenance: updating field descriptions as the data changes, adding new questions to the bank, and monitoring how the agent performs in production. Teams that treat an agent as a product to maintain, not a project to ship, are the ones whose agents stay accurate.

      Tableau MCP gives you the trusted foundation to build on. It brings the data, semantics and governance that teams have already built in Tableau to any agent, within any application. To learn more, explore the Tableau MCP documentation, including hosted Tableau MCP and tool scoping.

      Anyone who has watched a toddler build with wooden blocks has seen a hard research problem solved on a living room floor. I have spent years trying to get machines to do what a two-year-old does on instinct.

      Imagine one such child. She is stacking a tower of blocks, absorbed, and reaches for a piece that isn’t there. She pauses. She looks at the pile. She finds two smaller blocks that stack to the same height as the one she wanted, tests them, and keeps going.

      A few minutes later she hits an even harder problem and pauses again. A block has slipped into a gap at the base of the tower, too deep for her fingers to reach. Rearranging what she already has will not solve this one. So she looks around the room, picks up a wooden stick, and works the block free. Nobody handed it to her, she did this herself. 

      Four things happened in those two pauses.

      She noticed a gap. Before she could solve anything, she had to recognize that something was missing, which requires a working model of what the finished thing should look like.

      She gave herself a capability she did not have. The two blocks were a recombination of what was already in front of her. The stick was something else: her hands could not do the job, so she extended them.

      She got better at it. Over the following months, her improvisations got sharper. She learned which shapes bear weight, how wide a base needs to be, when a structure has gone far enough. Her towers improved because her judgment improved.

      And there was a fourth thing, which took me longer to see, because it is defined by its absence: what she didn’t do. At no point, however many towers she built, could she grow a third hand. That limit marks the boundary of learning.

      This is the era of self-evolving systems, where a machine can change what it is made of, and not just what it knows.

      The evolution of how machines learn

      Allow the professor in me a few minutes at the whiteboard, starting with five terms that get used loosely and interchangeably in conversations about AI research. They should not be, and knowing them makes everything that follows easier to see.

      • Learning is a system improving its performance using feedback, inside a process someone else designed.
      • Self-learning is a system identifying its own knowledge or performance gaps, seeking the feedback or experience it needs, and using it to improve.
      • Evolution is a change to a system’s architecture or learning mechanisms that produces new capabilities.
      • Self-evolution is a system identifying its own limitations and modifying its architecture, capabilities, or learning mechanisms to overcome them.
      • Recursive self-improvement (the term that’s getting the most attention lately) – goes one step further: the system improves not only its capabilities but also its ability to generate future improvements.

      Note the one word that separates each pair: “self.” It marks the point where the AI system, rather than a human, notices what is missing and acts on it.

      One more term before we start. A model’s weights are the billions of numerical settings inside it, adjusted a little at a time during training. Everything the model knows lives in those numbers, and nowhere else.

      Now on to how machines learn. 

      For roughly 50 years, machine learning has worked in a particular way, and it has worked well. A model encounters a high volume of example challenges or experiences. Some of its attempts earn rewards, and others are mistakes that draw corrections. Both become a signal. The signal adjusts the model’s weights, and the model gets better at its task. We have refined this loop many times over, and its shape has held: the knowledge in those weights changes, while the architecture holds still.

      Human beings learn much the same way. 

      If you’ve ever practiced a new language in an app like Duolingo, you’ve felt this loop firsthand: you attempt a sentence, the app rewards you or corrects you, and the next attempt comes a little easier. Each round of practice changes connections in the brain, and it is worth being precise about what. 

      We are born with a brain of a certain structure, and across a lifetime we modify its neural circuitry through a process called neuroplasticity. That change is considerable. Experience strengthens some synaptic connections and weakens others, builds new ones and prunes away the unused, and reorganizes entire functional networks around a newly learned skill. The brain grows, too, through childhood and adolescence. What remains relatively stable underneath all of that activity is the brain’s high-level architecture. We don’t spontaneously grow a second brain, develop an entirely new sensory system, or grow a third hand as in the toddler example.  Everything we call “learning” happens inside the bounds of our biology. The parallel to traditional machine learning is close: the model becomes more capable without fundamentally changing its computational architecture.

      Evolution operates on a different timescale and changes something deeper. Across generations, architecture itself shifts. Feathers that once kept small dinosaurs warm become the wings of a swallow, along with the neural wiring it needs to bank through a gust of wind. A patch of light-sensitive cells becomes an eye, and the brain reorganizes around everything the eye delivers. Architecture can shrink, too: vestigial structures that stop earning their keep, such as wisdom teeth in humans, become smaller or absent over time.

      Evolution changes more than the strength of connections. It changes what kind of nervous system there is to connect. The organism that emerges is built differently from its ancestor.

      I spent part of my Stanford years on exactly this boundary. In 2021, my colleagues and I published a paper in Nature Communications on embodied intelligence through learning and evolution. The idea was to run both processes at once in simulation: creatures whose body plans evolved across generations, while each individual creature learned to move through reinforcement learning within its own lifetime.

      A finding from this study has stayed with me and shaped how I think about enterprise AI today. We set a goal, and our AI system optimized for something we never specified, because the something turned out to be useful for the goal. In a simulation, that is a fascinating result. In a company, the stakes are much higher. A system that quietly optimizes for an objective nobody wrote down is how a pricing engine learns to misquote, or a claims process learns to approve what it should flag.

      All of which is why, when someone says an agent evolves, the useful question is which one they mean: 

      1. Is it learning, getting better within the structure it already has, or
      2. Is it evolving, changing the architectural structure itself?

      For a machine, the answer can be both, and more is in play than you might expect. Last year my colleagues and I published a survey of the frontiers of reasoning in large language models, and one of the clearest trends we tracked was the shift from standalone models to agentic systems.  A standalone model has one thing that can change, its weights. An agent has many: the tools it can call, the skills it can reuse, the specialists it can delegate to, the way it organizes its own work. Researchers call all of that surrounding apparatus the harness, and every part of it can learn and evolve.

      Here is where the biology stops being a guide. In living systems, learning and evolution run on different clocks. Learning takes a lifetime, and evolution takes generations. A machine has no such separation. A system can refine its reasoning from this morning’s work and give itself a module it lacked by the afternoon, running in one continuous process what biology splits across two very different timespans.

      The Self-Evolution Ladder: Toolmaker, Learner, Architect

      At Salesforce AI Research, we think about self-evolution as a ladder with three rungs. On the first, a system builds the tools it is missing. On the second, it improves its own reasoning. On the third, it helps design its own successor. Each rung builds on the one below it. The first is where our work is focused today, and the second and third are where that work leads. 

      Self-evolving systems are one of our key areas of focus this year, an area we believe will define enterprise AI, and my research team is pursuing all three rungs with a clear goal: improving Salesforce products faster and at scale.

      As we recount in a recent article (“Salesforce Releases R&D Agents That Improve Its AI Models”), a set of agents called SFR-AutoR&D improved the embedding model powering Data Cloud’s retrieval, the layer that helps agents find the right customer record, document, or case history.  And it did in about three days what has historically taken a team of scientists weeks. 

      Let’s step back and examine what this means. Let’s start at the bottom of the ladder.

      Level one: the Toolmaker.

      The system recognizes a missing capability and constructs it: a new API call, a new skill, a new routine added to its own harness. This is the toddler with the wooden stick, and it begins where she began, with gap awareness. A system that cannot tell what it does not know cannot build anything useful.

      In practice, this can be wonderfully ordinary. A system reconciling invoices meets a new supplier whose PDFs use a layout it has never seen, so it writes itself a parser, checks it against invoices a person already processed, and keeps it. Each fix is small, and each one stays.

      Our self-improvement framework MAS-Orchestra applies this idea to teams of agents. A lead agent divides the work among specialist agents, and every job leaves the team better equipped: it remembers what it learned, and its harness improves from one job to the next.

      The AutoR&D-Engineer agent behind that embedding model result applies the same instinct to software, working the way a careful research engineer would: it locates expensive work, forms a hypothesis, implements a new method, runs a controlled comparison, and keeps only what holds up.

      Level two: the Learner.

      Learning moves inward, into the model’s own reasoning. Two details matter here.

      The first is that this happens continuously. The older pattern was discrete: gather data, train, deploy, repeat. Here, doing the work and learning from it happen at the same time, the way a chef sharpens her technique in the middle of a busy dinner service.

      The second is that the tools and the reasoning improve together. Having a tool is not the same as knowing how to use it. After all, if I build myself a rocket, I still have to learn to fly it. A system that gives itself a new capability has to practice with it too, and the biggest gains come when the tool and the system’s own reasoning improve side by side. Memory makes this possible. Short-term memory lets the system adjust in the moment, the way a tennis player corrects her swing after one bad shot. Long-term memory lets it keep the lesson, so it never has to learn the same thing twice.

      TrainForge, another system from our team, takes this a step further: it invents new ways to train a model, tests each one against benchmarks it never trains on, and keeps only what wins. Its governing rule is one I would happily see adopted across our field: no improvement means no promotion.

      Level three: the Architect.

      This is the recursive frontier, where a system examines its own construction and produces a better version of itself. One model contributing to the design of its successor.

      We are beginning to see the early shape of this in research settings. The models that power TrainForge and AutoR&D-Engineer are themselves trained through our AutoInfra training service, and what those agents discover feeds the next version of the models. Version N helps produce version N plus one.

      This is the level where the toddler analogy fails completely. I can practice for 40 years and I will never redesign the architecture of my own brain. A system, in principle, can take part in redesigning its own.

      And this is where the difference between self-evolution and recursive self-improvement becomes concrete. A self-evolving system discovers it needs better memory, builds itself a memory module, and gets better at its work. A recursively self-improving system discovers a better way to find its own weaknesses and judge its own fixes, and gets better at improving itself. The first compounds capability, and the second compounds the rate at which capability arrives. Remember the toddler who could not grow a third hand? A system of this kind, indeed, could get better at growing one.

      Why this matters for your business

      All day long, employees are teaching your systems something, usually without noticing and almost always without anyone recording it. Every resolved case and every quiet correction an experienced employee makes to a draft answer is a lesson in how your business actually works.

      These lessons are specific to you. They reflect your customers, your products, your edge cases, your accumulated operational judgment. No off-the-shelf model has been trained on them.

      Today most of them evaporate the moment the ticket closes.

      A self-evolving system keeps them. A field technician finds a failure the manual never described and understands immediately why it happened. The system takes that observation, writes itself a diagnostic routine it did not have before, tests the routine against years of service records, and puts it to work. Within a week it catches the same failure at other sites. Improvement compounds, and it compounds from work the organization was doing anyway.

      That is the first rung, and it is where our work is focused today. The second and third raise the stakes. A system that improves how it reasons about your work, continuously, while doing it, is a different proposition from one retrained every quarter, and further out is a system that takes part in redesigning itself. At every level, one thing must stay true: you can see what changed, and you can prove it helped.

      A mistake a business system teaches itself does not stay small or contained. It repeats at scale, which is why nothing moves from our research into a Salesforce product without controlled comparisons, held-out evaluation and evidence before promotion. Those are the habits that should govern any system allowed to change itself inside your business.

      What evolves, and what never should

      I have spent much of this year inside the debate about AI safety: with policymakers, with customers, and through my work on the United Nations’ Independent International Scientific Panel on AI. In September, the panel published a brief on AI agents and the risk of losing human control, drawing on a real incident in which agents under evaluation found their way around network restrictions, cheated the evaluator, and tried to hide it. Much of the public conversation is still argued as though there were one question with one answer. But letting a system build itself a tool is one decision. Letting it rebuild how it thinks is another. They are not the same risk, and they should not get the same rules.

      What I would tell any leader deploying these systems is to decide deliberately what evolves and what stays fixed. Tools should evolve. Reasoning should improve. Architecture should change only where a person has judged it safe. What the business is for, what it will not do, and how it measures success should be the least changeable things in the stack, and people should set them. Capability can be improved. Values have to be held in place.

      Back on the living room carpet, the tower is finished, or as finished as towers ever get. She noticed what was missing, built what she needed, and got a little better at both. Then she knocks it down and starts again, reaching this time for a better stick.

      Our systems are learning to do something like that, and they will get faster at it. What they cannot do is decide what the tower is for. That part stays with us, and it should.

      • Bi-directional record sync: The publishing org chooses which objects and fields to share, and the subscribing org chooses what to accept and maps it to its own fields.       See the phased retirement schedule, Salesforce recommended alternatives by use case, and guidance on testing in a sandbox before you cut over.

      Replace S2S with Experience Cloud or Partner Connect in a partner scenario

      If the other org belongs to a partner, you have two options: Experience Cloud or Partner Connect, which requires Partner Cloud. The choice depends on whether the partner needs their own copy of the data.

      Use Experience Cloud when partners can work in your org

      The requirement is shared visibility into leads, opportunities, or cases, where partners update progress and you maintain one authoritative view.
